1:
Henry reads the departure as a farewell. Galilee had been the place of Christ’s upbringing and of most of his sermons and miracles, and he went under the character of a Galilean, a north-countryman from the least polite part of the nation; that was itself an instance of his humiliation. Now, these sayings finished, he leaves, and Henry marks the finality: unless the passage through Samaria and Galilee of Luke 17:11 came later, he never returned until after the resurrection. Christ did not go till his work there was done, and as faithful ministers are not taken out of the world, neither are they moved from a place before their testimony in it is finished (Revelation 11:7) — a comfort to any who follow providence instead of their own humours. Wesley states the bare fact without the application: from that time he walked no more in Galilee.

Chrysostom asks why Judaea now, after Christ had long avoided it out of regard to the envy of its leaders, and answers that the passion was near; even so he stops at the borders and does not go up to Jerusalem. Chrysostom also notices the alternation of word and work in these two verses. Christ neither teaches always nor always works wonders, but turns from one to the other, so that the wonders may win belief for his teaching and the teaching show what the wonders are good for; and because he healed men so as to help others through them, their cure became an occasion of knowledge of God in many, though the Pharisees it only hardened. Origen hears a further claim in the formula of the transition. To finish one’s words is to leave nothing of the matter unsaid, and that, he argues, holds of no one else — not Moses, not the prophets — but of Jesus only, who came to put an end to things and supply what the law left defective. Robertson weighs the same clause as grammar: it is a formula Matthew uses to close his great blocks of sayings, as at 7:28, 11:1 and 13:53, and the verb rendered departed means to lift and shift, intransitive only here and in the last of those three. Gill supplies the content of the sayings now ended: humility, offences, the manner of reproving an offender and the forgiving of him.

Where exactly the road ran is disputed. Barnes has him cross the river to avoid Samaria and travel south along the east bank through Peraea, old territory of Reuben, Gad and Manasseh. Robertson agrees that Galileans commonly took that way, adding from Luke 17:11 that this journey skirted Samaria as well. Clarke dissents over the preposition, holding that beyond Jordan here means by the side of Jordan, since Jericho lies seven miles west of the water, in the one journey to the final passover Matthew records. Lightfoot grants that the phrase could bear the eastern sense, with a parallel in Josephus, but prefers Mark’s plainer wording at Mark 10:1. Ellicott steps back from route to interval: the verse spans a whole Peræan ministry, Luke 9:51 to 18:30, and the visits of John 7:2 and John 10:22. Raban divides the ministry itself, east of Jordan first and afterwards westward by Jericho and Bethphage to Jerusalem, and separates Judaea proper, the portion of Judah and Benjamin, from the whole land that bore the name.

On the healing, Pseudo-Chrysostom sees a father setting out on a long journey and leaving his children a pledge of his love. Origen presses that it happened where baptism had been given, since baptism is where spiritual sickness is truly cured, and separates crowds who merely followed from Matthew, who arose and followed. Hilary finds the Gentiles admitted at that frontier to the pardon prepared for the Jews. Clarke sorts the motives of the throng: instruction, cure, curiosity, entrapment.
3:
Henry notes that they ask to tempt, not to be taught: Christ had already spoken against the practice in Galilee, and a fresh refusal could turn a people fond of that liberty against him. Jerome puts the trap as a syllogism with two horns — allow the putting away and he contradicts his own preaching of chastity; forbid it and he is impious against Moses. Robertson, Barnes, Clarke and Lightfoot all place the dilemma in the schools: Shammai permitted divorce for unchastity alone, Hillel for any passing dislike — for Clarke, any other woman who pleased the husband better. Ellicott supplies the political danger, since in Peræa the tetrarch’s own divorce lay near. Clarke names the escape: answering from Moses rather than either school, Christ confounded their devices.

Henry traces the reply in three steps: one female made for one male, so Adam had no other to take; the leaving of father and mother, a tie nearer than the filial; and the one flesh, so that a man’s wife is himself, and none hates his own flesh. Calvin reduces it to two heads, creation’s order serving as law and the later toleration as concession to an intractable nation, and hears in the number a verdict against polygamy, as Malachi had (Malachi 2:15). Clarke, taking cleave from gluing, notes that a well-glued board breaks sooner in the whole wood than at the joint, and takes one flesh to include the child compounded of both (Genesis 2:24). Robertson observes that the sentence says what God joined, not whom, the yoking verb in a timeless aorist. Ellicott remarks that the essence of the bond is thus made to rest on the natural fact of union rather than on contract or ceremony.

On the writing of divorcement every voice separates command from permission. Henry calls it an allowance framed to restrain rather than countenance, hedged with formalities that forbade haste (Deuteronomy 24:1). Barnes agrees that Moses only regulated a universal custom, obliging an angry husband to deliberate. Lightfoot presses that hardness of heart in scripture more often names obduracy toward God than unkindness to a wife, and would render the preposition as to: Moses added divorce to their hardness, as a punishment. Ellicott generalises: the same concession may explain the Law’s tolerance of polygamy and slavery, and a nation calling itself Christian may sink low enough to need concessive legislation still. Jerome holds that fornication alone divides the flesh, and that remarriage is barred so long as the first partner lives; Origen asks what follows if the wife be no adulteress but a poisoner or child-killer; Pseudo-Chrysostom answers that wills and not bodies make or dissolve the union; Calvin insists the right is mutual, the husband no more lord of his body than the wife. Robertson defends the exception Matthew alone records against McNeile, who dates it to a later practice.

The recoil of the disciples — better then not to marry — Henry calls sullen, children throwing away what they have because denied what they want; Calvin calls it base ingratitude, and reproaches Jerome by name for gathering pagan slanders against a divine institution. On the three eunuchs Hilary assigns the causes nature, violence and choice; Chrysostom insists the third means a putting away of evil thoughts, since to cut off a limb is to undertake the work of murderers and open a door to the Manichaeans; Clarke and Barnes look to the Essenes, and Clarke recalls that Origen took the words on himself literally. Ellicott grants Rome and the monastic founders their ideal, faulting only its imposition on those unable to realise it. Calvin denies that celibacy is in itself a virtue, excusing it on the single ground of freedom for better employments (1 Corinthians 7:7). Gill and Wesley agree the gift is given to few, whom Wesley bids receive it joyfully.
13:
Pseudo-Chrysostom explains the timing: the discourse had been of chastity, and the hearers, supposing that only bodily purity had been approved, brought the purest bodies they had. He finds the rebuke sharper for following so soon on the child Christ had set in the midst, and asks who could be worthy if simple infancy were thrust away — if they prove saints, why hinder sons from their Father; if sinners, why sentence them before any fault appears? The motive of the rebuke is variously read. Jerome lays it to an imperfect faith, which supposed their Master would be wearied like other men; Chrysostom to a jealous regard for his dignity; Robertson thinks the Twelve believed they were doing him a kindness, having no vision of his love for children; Ellicott ties it to the saying just spoken: men who had heard the eunuch life honoured could take mothers and infants only for an interruption of prayer. Origen turns it inward: the more advanced, before they have learnt the way of righteousness that is for children, rebuke those who bring the unlearned, and must learn to be babes to babes, as he who was in the form of God was made a babe.

On the laying on of hands Remigius recalls the old custom of bringing little children to aged men for benediction by hand or tongue; Barnes, Clarke and Wesley trace the rite to Jacob’s hands on the sons of Joseph (Genesis 48:14) and read it as a consecration, the person thereafter held sacred property; the Gloss notes that the hands were laid while men held them, signifying that the grace of his aid was needed. Henry adds that the gesture mingles love and familiarity with authority, and that whom Christ prays for in heaven he lays his hand upon by his Spirit. Calvin presses what the act presumed: those who brought them must have been persuaded the Spirit was at his disposal, and since the less is blessed by the better (Hebrews 7:7) they allowed him the honour of the highest Prophet, though they had not grasped his office. Gill enters a caution about the age: the words used do not always mean newborns, and these were called and came.

Of such is the kingdom divides the witnesses. Jerome marks the pronoun: of such, not of these, because disposition and not years decided the judgment, the reward being promised to whoever keeps the like innocence. Barnes goes further, that the phrase means persons resembling children in temper, of whom the church is composed, and that although he hopes all infants saved, the passage was not framed to teach it. Clarke takes it the other way, the kingdom being literally composed of such, and the contrary doctrine of non-elect infants’ damnation sprung from Moloch. Henry reads the children of believing parents into the visible church, and takes it ill of any who forbid them the water; Lightfoot, pressing that believers brought them and not Jews who despised him, concludes that their infants were disciples as much as their parents. Calvin uses the passage as a shield against the Anabaptists: baptism being the pledge of forgiveness and adoption, it may not be denied to those whom God adopts, who are renewed by the Spirit according to the capacity of their age. Ellicott finds here the true warrant of the English baptismal office, surer than doubtful passages in the Acts and Epistles, and asks why those capable of spiritual blessing then should be thought incapable now.

Hilary alone allegorises the infants as the Gentiles, forbidden by disciples still zealous for Israel, who would receive the Spirit by laid-on hands when the Law had ceased. Henry hears finality in the departure, as though enough had been done once the rights of the lambs were settled; Clarke places it simply, out of the country beyond Jordan toward Jericho.
16:
Gill and Calvin take him for a civil magistrate, and Henry, since youth would bar a man from the bench, infers abilities beyond his years. Ellicott presses the anonymity: a conspicuous man goes unnamed, as the woman with the spikenard does until John names her, and ventures that the ruler was Lazarus — a wealthy household, friends among the chief rulers, a sister who believed in eternal life, the one thing lacking answering the one thing needful of Luke 10:42. Jerome finds him young, rich and proud, asking as one who tempts, and reads his which? as insidious, since he could read the commandments himself. Chrysostom will not call him a hypocrite: Mark has him running and kneeling, and reports that Jesus looked on him and loved him; it is unsafe to decide uncertain cases, above all in blame. Calvin agrees he came from a desire of instruction, not treacherously like the scribes; what hindered him was blind confidence in his works. Robertson asks whether the question betrayed proud complacency or pathetic despair, and answers both.

Clarke marshals the manuscripts for a different reading — why dost thou question me concerning that good thing? — which Griesbach admitted, and notes that the anti-trinitarian argument built on the common form collapses if it stands. Augustine, harmonising the forms, has Christ point past the title given to the form of a son of man toward the one God. Here Henry and Calvin part. Henry holds that Christ would have him either know him God or not call him good, the correction being a lesson in transferring to God all praise given us. Calvin rejects that refinement: the essence of the Godhead is not maintained here, only the authority of the doctrine — thou callest me good falsely unless thou own I have come from God. Barnes takes it for a reproof of flattering titles, no disclaimer of divinity; Wesley insists the answer is plain and serious, not ironical.

Why only the second table is recited draws three answers. Calvin says observance of the first is readily feigned, so the second serves better for scrutiny, and places the fifth commandment in that table against Josephus. Lightfoot notes the pattern, that where the whole law is named it is the second table that gets exemplified (Romans 13:9, James 2:8), charity to a neighbour being the top of religion. Henry adds that a merely moral man is no complete Christian while an immoral man is none at all: our light burns in love to God but shines in love to our neighbour. Raban sees two lives set out, the active belonging to the Law and the contemplative to the Gospel.

The command to sell divides them. Jerome, answering Vigilantius, denies that those who keep their estates and dole out the income do better than those who sell at once; Remigius marks every word, not consume but sell, not some as Ananias did but all, and to the poor, not to neighbours or the rich; Pseudo-Augustine grants discriminate alms good and the single stripping better. Augustine will not shut out the hired multitude who merely fed the hungry, and finds parting with what we own the harder thing, like losing a limb. Lightfoot answers that Christ used the nation’s own idiom of perfection — its casuists capped alms at a fifth of an estate — to try a man who boasted of keeping the law. Wesley calls the direction particular, never meant for a rule: necessary for him, for many of us a sin; Ellicott, binding in spirit not letter, names schools, hospitals and missions. Origen turns possessions into the acts of the mind, to be sold off to the virtues. Henry names covetousness the rock he split on, crediting him the honesty of going rather than pretending; Ellicott finds hope in the sorrow, since a worldling would have sneered.
23:
Chrysostom aims the saying not at wealth but at those enslaved by it, and at comforting poor disciples; he marks the move from hard to impossible, and finds in beheld a merciful eye. Hilary agrees that having riches is no sin — who could supply the saints’ necessities with nothing to give? — though growing rich is a dangerous toil. Raban grants the distinction between having and loving, yet calls it safer to do neither. Remigius takes Mark’s them that trust in riches as the sense: God does not bring the covetous in as he is, but converts him first. Jerome says hard and not impossible: difficulty marks infrequency, not exclusion. Augustine, noting how few the rich are beside the poor, takes all who merely wish for riches to be counted among them; Clarke so defines him, as one who keeps the surplus of his household’s need while the poor starve.

Henry reads the figure: a rich man carries a load that is another’s, had from others, spent for others, shortly left to others. On the camel Calvin breaks from the rest, taking the word for a sailor’s rope, not the animal. Ellicott answers that no manuscript gives that word, which the best scholars think coined for this verse, and Robertson calls every such escape jejune, since Christ goes on to say impossible. Lightfoot and Clarke supply the school idiom: no man is shown a palm tree of gold or an elephant passing a needle, and Pombeditha was mocked for making one pass. The Gloss offers a Jerusalem gate called the needle’s eye, which a camel passed only unloaded and kneeling; Ellicott knows its Syrian parallel and judges it unproven and unnecessary. Pseudo-Chrysostom allegorises: the camel is the Gentile soul humped with idolatry, the needle the Son of God, fine at the point of his divinity and thicker in his flesh.

What was this all, asks Chrysostom — the reeds, the net, the boat? — answering that Peter asked not to parade his sacrifice but to bring in the poor, lest any think perfection closed to him. Origen credits the will rather than the price, Peter inquiring like a victorious athlete after his prizes. Jerome notes that Crates and other philosophers despised riches too, so the weight falls on have followed thee. Gregory adds that whoever forsakes his possessions will appear as judge with the Judge. What the regeneration means divides them four ways. Hilary takes it of the laver of baptism, which the Law could not bestow. Pseudo-Chrysostom and Calvin place it at the first advent, Calvin distinguishing the reign’s beginning from its completion, Pseudo-Chrysostom making each Christian who receives an apostle’s word his throne. Lightfoot recalls them from the grosser Jewish hope: what is renewed is manners and doctrine, not the fabric of the world. Barnes, Clarke and Robertson keep it for the restitution at the judgment, Clarke repunctuating to join it to the Son of man’s sitting. Augustine reads the twelve as standing for all who judge, else Paul would want a throne, and denies that Levi escapes as the thirteenth tribe. Chrysostom, Ellicott and Wesley observe the one throne left empty: the promise was to those who followed, and Judas proved unworthy.

Of the hundredfold Jerome protests that a literal reading would shame the promise in the matter of wives, and takes carnal things exchanged for spiritual; Ellicott has relationships multiply by spiritual sympathy, and hears Mark’s with persecutions as too strange not to have been spoken. Calvin faces the objection that exiles recover nothing, and answers that the little God sweetens is better than abundance held outside Christ. On the reversal, Origen and Clarke think of Israel and the Gentiles, Origen adding that angels once first were made last by sin; Remigius applies it to the ruler, first by the Law, last by his substance; Raban, to all who begin in zeal and cool.
